items.title: We didn’t lose the South to voter suppression alone. We lost it because we stopped building.
items.summary: For years, we have treated attacks on voting rights as isolated battles. They are not. They are the harvest of a long-term investment strategy—and our failure to match it is a choice we are still making. For years, many of us have treated attacks on voting rights as a series of isolated battles. A restrictive voting law here. A gerrymandered district there. A Supreme Court ruling that strips away protections that generations of Americans bled and marched and died to secure. We respond. We litigate. We mobilize. And then we move on to the next fight, rarely pausing long enough to ask the harder question: What if we have been looking at this the wrong way? What if the real story is not just what they are doing to these communities, but what we have refused to do for them? Over the past several weeks, I have been traveling throughout the South with the March On for Freedom national voter registration tour, organized by Registration Nation Action Fund and its partners. From Natchez, Mississippi, to Greenville, South Carolina; Dallas, Texas; Tallahassee, Florida; and rural Georgia, I have witnessed something that rarely makes its way into our national political conversation: enthusiasm, determination, and communities eager to participate, but too often without the sustained infrastructure to translate that energy into lasting political power. “We called these places red states. The people living there called them home, and kept organizing anyway, with or without us.”

items.title: Preserving the body politic against anti-immigration surges on Election Day
items.summary: With increasing ICE presence designed to suppress, surveil, profile, and intimidate voters to stay at home, it is crucial that communities mobilize to support targeted, vulnerable members. The body is political. It acts as a physical plane where intangible legislative ideas are made visible. Certain phenotypes, or physical characteristics, can either trigger suspicion or secure the safety of privilege. In a democracy, the body votes for itself, and a healthy society promises every member the right to seek protection through policy. When the state makes certain bodies afraid to appear in public, it also makes them afraid to vote. On the morning of Monday, October 5, 18-year-old Mayrin was on her way to class at Allan Hancock College in Santa Maria, California, with her father at the wheel. At about 9:45 am, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained him in a campus parking lot. It was the first day California’s ballot drop boxes opened, and an adjoining lot in the same parking area was an active ballot drop-off site. Voters had to pass through the area where agents were making the arrest to reach the box. By the end of the day, masked ICE officers had arrested at least 17 people in Santa Maria and nearby Guadalupe. When the state makes certain bodies afraid to appear in public, it also makes them afraid to vote.

items.title: One in seven Louisiana voters is now “inactive.”
items.summary: In 18 months, Louisiana's inactive voter list grew from 178,000 to 450,000—and the burden is falling hardest on voters of color. These are not people who drifted away from democracy. They are people the system moved to the sidelines. In January 2025, 178,395 Louisiana voters were listed as “inactive”—six percent of the rolls. By July 2026, that number was 450,086. More than one in seven registered voters in the state now carries the label. Inactive is not the same as removed. But it is the step before removal, and adds friction at the exact moment a voter shows up to cast a ballot. These are not people who drifted away from democracy. They are people the system moved to the sidelines. Of the 450,000 voters listed as inactive in Louisiana, 52,981 cast a ballot in November 2024. Nearly 84,000 more voted in 2020 or 2022. It turns an unanswered envelope into a change in voting status. And mail is a blunt instrument. It doesn’t reach people who moved across town, who share a mailbox, who don’t read English, or who set aside official-looking letters they assume are junk. Secretary of State Nancy Landry has said the increase stems from a 2024 law that let her office send address-confirmation mailings to anyone who hadn’t voted in 10 or more years. This cycle was the first time the tool was used. Voters who didn’t respond were moved to inactive. On paper, that sounds like routine housekeeping. Federal law requires states to make a reasonable effort to keep their rolls current, and outdated lists carry real costs: mail sent to empty addresses or inflated registration counts, for example.

items.title: A grant isn’t always the right tool: The case for program-related investments
items.summary: Is philanthropy using all the tools in its toolbox to drive social change? Program-related investments, which allow foundations to deploy loans, equity, and other repayable capital for charitable purposes, can provide regenerative capital that benefits nonprofits and helps foundations expand their reach. Yet only a small fraction of foundations use them.

items.title: North Carolina is the canary in the coalmine for attacks on our democracy—and a model for how we fight back
items.summary: North Carolina is a testing ground for repressive policies that are rolled out across the country, from voter suppression to gerrymandering. For years, North Carolina has been the canary in the coal mine for voter suppression, and a testing ground for policies that are rolled out across the South. North Carolinians are currently voting under the weight of a discriminatory photo voter ID law, gerrymandered districts, severe cuts to early voting days, and removal of key early voting locations. To understand where we are now, we must look back at our state’s history. North Carolina is the site of the only successful coup d’état in United States history. The 1898 Wilmington Massacre was a violent and concerted effort by White supremacists to overthrow the city’s elected multiracial government. In the late 1800’s, Wilmington had a thriving Black population with business owners, skilled tradesmen, lawyers, and doctors, and three of the city’s 10 aldermen were Black. On Election Day in 1898, militiamen and White mobs took to the streets and murdered a still unconfirmed number of Black people to prevent them from voting, before burning the city’s only Black newspaper office to the ground. The mob issued a ‘White Declaration of Independence’, held local officials at gunpoint until they resigned their seats, and ran prominent Black families from their homes. Estimates of the number of people killed range from 60 to over 200. Before the massacre, Wilmington had a Black population of 56 percent; today, it stands at 14.5 percent.

items.title: Who gets to decide who decides? The power problem inside participatory grantmaking
items.summary: How is authority distributed when communities participate in funding decisions? To answer this, we must examine who sets the terms, who controls the resources, and who has the authority to change the rules. Participatory grantmaking begins with a deceptively simple question: What would happen if people directly affected by funders’ decisions helped decide how resources were used? Some foundations involve community members in setting priorities, evaluating applications, and making funding decisions. Others invite communities to shape a fund and recommend recipients while retaining final authority through an executive or board. Both may involve participation, but they distribute institutional power differently. The Participatory Grantmaking Community (PGMC) defines participatory grantmaking as ceding funding decision-making power—including decisions about strategy and criteria—to the communities funders aim to serve. This distinction echoes Sherry Arnstein’s 1969 “Ladder of Citizen Participation,” which identified consultation as a form of participation that can give people a voice without giving them control. The central question is not simply whether communities are included, but what authority they actually hold. NPQ has previously covered participatory grantmaking, including in Kelley Buhles’ “A Primer for Participatory Grantmaking.” This article builds on that coverage by examining how authority is distributed when communities participate in funding decisions.

items.title: After we were seen
items.summary: At a campaign rally this October, with the November 3 midterms approaching, Donald Trump explained why he insisted on calling Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, “Mohammed.” Someone had corrected him and Trump told the crowd, “I’m the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want.” Mohamed is part of El-Sayed’s full name, though Abdul is the name he uses. Trump knew the distinction and made a performance of overruling it. He then called the candidate a “radical jihadist.” There is a disturbing presumption behind the joke: that the powers of Trump’s office extend even to deciding a man’s name and manipulating his reputation without regard for facts or norms. On October 25, Trump went further, comparing the effort to keep El-Sayed out of the Senate to passengers resisting the September 11 hijackers. I began to wonder how much an election could truly change about American power when those living beneath America’s drones had no vote.

items.title: What 250 years of Black Muslim traditions can teach us
items.summary: Black Muslims across the US continually faced intersectional invisibility and are often excluded from Black, Arab and Muslim narratives. Author Maryam Abdul-Kareem speaks to what Black Muslims can offer to liberatory movements as well as philanthropy when we tap into our shared humanness. The first Muslim ban was not signed under the Trump administration in 2017. On Christmas morning in 1521, on a Hispaniola plantation governed by the violence of Christopher Columbus’s son, roughly 20 enslaved Africans, many of them Wolof Muslims from Senegambia, a region in West Africa that spans Senegal and The Gambia, staged the earliest recorded slave revolt in the Americas. In the decades that followed, the Spanish crown issued decrees barring the importation of enslaved Black Muslims, judged too rebellious and too literate to be safely owned. The scholar Margarita Rosa has documented this history as part of a long pattern of Muslim resistance to enslavement. Historian Sylviane Diouf calls the 1526 decree the first Muslim ban, which was 400 years before the phrase entered American politics, the beginning of a criminal narrative constructed around Muslims for refusing to be owned or exterminated.

items.title: Wisdom workers: The capacity nonprofits must learn to recognize and preserve
items.summary: How nonprofits can recognize, leverage, and retain the wisdom workers who are key to building their capacity. A telephone-company troubleshooter called me. She was five years retired and asked about volunteer work at the nonprofit hospital where I was employed. Buried in work, I needed someone to read an audit report that suggested a contractor had misused restricted funds for three years. It was boring, dense, technical work that required knowing what “routine” looks like well enough to spot when something wasn’t. Leaning on her willingness to support, I accepted her help. She read it in 48 hours and mapped out exactly where the misuse had occurred, how long it had been going on, and what to do about it. Most organizations that could use help may never think to ask for it. They know how to onboard labor, but, in my experience, many organizations no longer know how to recognize those who not only want to volunteer their talent but also their wisdom to increase the organization’s capacity. Labor is what you pay someone to do: tasks, hours, deliverables, transactional by design. Wisdom begins where a job description ends, moving past compliance into an unprompted sense of responsibility. It is what a person does because they hold responsibility for something larger than their assigned role. A laborer asks, “Is this what I was asked to do?” The wisdom worker asks, “Is this right?” A laborer asks, “Can I get this done?” A steward asks, “Should this be done at all?”

items.title: No bond, no judge: The case that could redefine immigrant rights in the United States
items.summary: What is at stake in an upcoming Supreme Court decision extends beyond administrative procedure. The decision could determine how far executive authority reaches. As immigration returns to the center of the US political debate, the Supreme Court is preparing to decide a case that could fundamentally reshape the nation’s immigration detention system. At issue is whether the federal government can hold immigrants in deportation proceedings without granting them a bond hearing before an immigration judge. Immigrant rights advocates argue that what is at stake extends far beyond an administrative procedure. The decision could determine how far executive authority reaches when depriving noncitizens of their liberty, and what constitutional protections remain available to them while their immigration cases are pending. At the center of this legal battle is the case of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian national whose circumstances have become a critical test of the federal government’s detention powers. After entering the United States around 2004 or 2005 without formal inspection, Barbosa da Cunha spent the next two decades building a life in the country, raising a family, running a small construction business, applying for asylum, and obtaining authorization to work. He had no criminal record. In September 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested him in Massachusetts on his way to work. Shortly afterward, the Department of Homeland Security initiated deportation proceedings against him.

items.title: Democracy denied: lessons from incarcerated communities and US territorial residents
items.summary: What can the distinct experiences of Puerto Rico and communities impacted by incarceration reveal about the structural barriers to democratic participation? And what is philanthropy’s role in dismantling them? It’s hard to convey the power of witnessing two groups, often hidden and made invisible, be seen and centered. In 2025, I was facilitating a cycle of New Profit’s Unlocked Futures program, a cohort-based portfolio investing in transforming the US criminal legal system, where we convene and provide strategic support for organizations led by formerly incarcerated and directly impacted leaders. That year, we chose to hold our final convening as a cohort in Puerto Rico—a choice years in the making, as I had been reflecting on the similarities between the experiences of the US territories and those impacted by the US carceral system. Witnessing these similarities play out in real time would prove transformative to me, the participants, and how we might conceptualize what it means to work toward a more democratic United States.

items.title: What happens when a fiscal sponsor shuts down?
items.summary: The closure of the High Desert Community Foundation fiscal sponsorship program forces nonprofits to consider what happens when community projects depend on a shared nonprofit structure—and when that structure gets taken away. The High Desert Community Foundation (HDCF) has announced it will end its fiscal sponsorship program on December 31, 2026, with operations expected to cease by the end of June 2027. This means the foundation’s sponsored projects will need to establish their own independent nonprofit status or find another fiscal sponsor. HDCF’s decision, announced on July 30, affects more than just the foundation itself. The foundation had previously stated that its sponsorship program supports more than 30 community projects in youth development, healthcare access, food insecurity, and services for underserved communities. HDCF provides the projects with the financial, legal, and organizational structure needed that allows them to operate. The closure of the funding program forces nonprofits and community project leaders to consider what happens when multiple community projects depend on a shared nonprofit structure, and what happens when that structure gets taken away. Creating a nonprofit involves substantial paperwork and ongoing compliance, plus it takes time and money. Fiscal sponsorships allow a project to operate through an existing nonprofit organization rather than having the project create its own tax-exempt status. Fiscal sponsorships can provide the legal and financial infrastructure behind a project, such as managing funds, receiving charitable contributions, handling the accounting, and providing compliance support.

items.title: Listening Is Not the ‘Soft’ Option (Blog)
items.summary: To make measurement meaningful and real, social change organizations must cultivate a listening orientation to go beyond "objective" measurements of impact. Any organization trying to improve people’s lives has to answer two questions, one about experience and the other about outcomes. Are we serving people well? And are their lives actually getting better? The organizations that create the most lasting social change treat them as one practice rather than a choice between two. It’s easy to lose sight of the difference between measurement sophistication and organizational seriousness about that measure. They are not the same thing. A sophisticated study that no one acts on is not serious. A simple one that changes a decision is. With the rise of customer “listening” in social change organizations, including wider use of mainstream metrics like customer satisfaction scores and Net Promoter Score®, a hierarchy has quietly formed between measuring outcomes and listening. Because the hierarchy ranks methods by sophistication—or privileges “objectivity” over “subjectivity”—it mistakes that for seriousness. Thus, while randomized trials and quasi-experimental designs sit at the top, customer listening is seen as a “soft” option, at best; at worst, it is viewed as impact washing.

items.title: The New Nonprofit Visibility Gap (Blog)
items.summary: AI is narrowing the pathways available to donors for finding nonprofits worthy of support. Nonprofits and the social sector must act to ensure that donors can make fully informed decisions. Picture someone troubled by an article about growing numbers of children dying from preventable causes. Motivated to help, she decides to donate, but she is a charity novice and doesn’t know where to turn. A few years ago, she might have opened a search engine and typed, “Where should I donate to save children’s lives?” The query would have generated a long list of links. The donor might have spent an hour clicking through charity ratings, reading annual reports, comparing local and global options, and weighing her values against the evidence. The path was imperfect, but it left room for discovery. Now imagine the same scenario today. Bypassing search, our donor consults AI chat interfaces. One recommends donating to GiveWell’s top charities—Against Malaria Foundation, Helen Keller International, Malaria Consortium. Another recommends donating to GiveWell’s Top Charities Fund directly. The answers differ slightly, but the tools converge on the same destination. They do not surface other ways of having impact: community health workers supporting underserved families, early research on a pediatric disease, or a smaller global health group that the major charity evaluators have not yet rated. Both close with a version of the same line: “If I were making one donation, I’d make it this one.”

items.title: Creating Climate Policy That Works Requires Community Data (Blog)
items.summary: Portland residents explained what makes a building livable in a heat wave. Their responses became the basis for statewide climate policy. In June 2021, a heat dome settled over the Pacific Northwest and Portland reached 116 degrees. Nearly 100 Oregonians died of heat-related illness, most of them at home. By then, the Coalition of Communities of Color (CCC) had a long-standing partnership with the City of Portland and was collaborating with community members to design building and energy policy. A community policy workshop took place shortly after the heat dome, bringing residents’ recent experiences of extreme heat directly into the conversation. CCC asked community members what they needed to stay cool and what it was costing them. During these conversations, attendees said the extreme heat wave was stressful. They said it forced impossible choices. Residents said they felt like they were being chased by the mafia. Community members described what they wanted their city to protect, and the values they surfaced became the HEART Standards: Health, Equitable energy, Anti-displacement, Resilience, and Temperature, a community-developed framework for shaping building policy. These standards anchor Portland’s approach to the buildings its residents live in and the climate-resilient policies designed to protect them.

items.title: A new tax credit could change where education donors give
items.summary: A provision in the 2025 tax overhaul provides individuals a tax credit of up to $1,700 for giving to a qualified scholarship granting organization. Beginning January 1, 2027, the IRS will offer a tax credit for donations made to scholarship funds for K-12 private schools and educational services supporting students in these grades. This is the first time the federal government has offered a tax credit for charitable giving. It is also the first time the IRS has offered a tax advantage for giving to a particular category of giving — scholarships. As part of the 2025 tax overhaul, the provision provides individuals a tax credit of up to $1,700 for giving to a qualified scholarship granting organization (SGO). Unlike a charitable deduction, which reduces the amount of income that can be taxed, a tax credit reduces the amount of total taxes you owe dollar for dollar. In many states SGOs will be brand-new entities. The IRS released an initial set of rules on the new provisions, but questions remain about how SGOs will partner with schools and educational nonprofits providing services and whether the new credit will reduce the amount of money donors contribute to other charitable causes.

items.title: Who’s paying to protect democracy? Meet the 10 biggest donors.
items.summary: The list includes some very wealthy U.S. philanthropists who tend to give big but are not nationally known. Giving to democracy is on the rise among some wealthy donors and has surged since 2021, according to a Chronicle tally of gifts of $1 million or more.. Rich donors have made 18 gifts totaling $369.2 million to democracy programs since 2006, but $266.5 million of that, or 72 percent, was given from 2021 through 2025. Though the issue is gaining traction, it remains a small percentage of overall giving by this group, which tends to favor education and health care. Programs affiliated with universities received the majority of these gifts over that five-year period. Three went to other types of groups, including the ACLU, Interfaith America, and New York Historical. The largest gift — $59 million to the University of Southern California — was made by Leonard Schaeffer, the founder of the Wellpoint health insurance company. Schaeffer is a professor of public policy there and served in the late 1970s as head of the Health Care Financing Administration during the Carter administration. items.title: Your event may cost more than it raises. Here’s how to check.
items.summary: Inertia keeps many fundraising events running long past their prime. Experts explain how to let go. Amber Melanie Smith founded Activate Good in college after making a cross-country trip with the goal of volunteering in 20 states. Its mission: to increase volunteerism by connecting people with likeminded causes and nonprofits. Early on, an excited supporter suggested a fashion show as a fundraising event for Activate Good. The gung-ho volunteer helped raise more than $25,000 at the event — which Smith felt was a good amount for a small nonprofit. Here are some questions to ask when trying to figure out if your event still makes sense: Years passed, and Activate Good continued to hold the fashion show, but it ate up excessive time and staff energy and had no connection to its mission to encourage volunteerism. “There was a moment I was sitting in a U-Haul truck at 2 in the morning by myself, the executive director, returning everything to our storage unit, and I just felt like there had to be a better way,” Smith says. Not every nonprofit leader ends up returning event rentals after midnight, but the pattern is common: Nonprofits start a fundraiser, inertia sets in, and the event continues for years, even when it’s taking up unreasonable amounts of staff time and is no longer serving the organization. Fundraising events that aren’t serving your mission or raising money need to go the way of the dodo bird, experts say. However, getting rid of them can prove tough.

items.title: Podcast: Give in a way that lets the money do good again
items.summary: Giving to nonprofits can combine grant making and investing. There’s a difference between traditional grant making and traditional investing, and donors, foundations, and DAF holders aren’t limited to one or the other. That’s according to Tracy Palandjian, co-founder and CEO of Social Finance, which has an unusual structure: It’s a nonprofit that is also a registered investment adviser and deploys capital across a spectrum of tools most philanthropists never consider. In this podcast interview with Phil Buchanan, president of the Center for Effective Philanthropy, Palandjian walks through how this works in practice. Her framework for donors sitting on new wealth: give a lot, give effectively, and, where possible, give in a way that lets the money come back and do good again. The Chronicle of Philanthropy appreciates the opportunity to share this podcast and wants to note that the interview was conducted by Center for Effective Philanthropy with no involvement from the Chronicle’s newsroom.

items.title: How one Texas city turns community input into local change
items.summary: In Galveston, nonprofits, funders, and government are collaborating on a community-developed plan to transform the city. Inside the commercial-scale kitchen at a former elementary school in Galveston, Tex., Erica Delgadillo points with excitement to huge ovens, stainless steel countertops, and rolling racks of sheet pans. Here she plans to train aspiring entrepreneurs on the skills they’ll need to work in the food industry. Start by listening. Vision Galveston gathered input from 8,500 residents to create a 78-point plan for improving the city. Build relationships across sectors. Bring funders, government officials, and nonprofit leaders together around shared goals, drawing on their different resources and expertise. Learn from other communities. Rather than reinvent the wheel, visit cities that have tackled similar challenges. Pair quick wins with long-term ambitions. Small, easy-to-fix improvements like home repairs and air conditioner installation, help maintain community engagement while Vision Galveston tackles larger challenges like housing and greenspace. Develop local talent. Public pitch contests and leadership training help residents develop ideas, build connections, and take a more active role in shaping their community.

items.title: Anthropic’s $300 billion promise leaves nonprofit leaders asking who decides and when
items.summary: Anthropic commits 20 percent of shares to the public good, but critics question how much will actually go to charities. In posts on its website and filings ahead of its upcoming public offering of stock, Anthropic has made an extraordinary commitment to “the public good.” It announced that 5 percent of shares will be put into an LLC, the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, subject to shareholder approval. Anthropic’s seven co-founders have also pledged that they will donate 80 percent of their shares to philanthropic causes. Anthropic said those two moves — plus the company’s generous matching program for employees who give to charity — will result in roughly 20 percent of company shares going to the public good. “There is no sure or simple path to progress, and the best outcomes are not preordained,” Daniela Amodei, Anthropic’s co-founder and president, wrote in the company’s first public-benefit report this month. “So we’re putting meaningful resources behind achieving those outcomes.” But some nonprofit and philanthropic leaders are concerned about vague language and other uncertainties. For example, the securities filing notes that the 80 percent pledge is not binding. Other leaders are excited about the possibility of hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into philanthropy that could profoundly change the sector.

items.title: Big money is flooding elections, and grant makers have walked away
items.summary: Despite widespread bipartisan concern over money in politics, grant makers have largely abandoned the issue. Keep up with everything happening in The Commons by signing up for our monthly newsletter. This spring, when Pew Research asked Americans what issues were most important to them, money in politics ranked at the top, regardless of party affiliation. It was a surprising finding, given the country’s deep polarization on many political issues and animosity toward members of the opposing party. Pew’s survey found that 74 percent of Americans identify money in politics as “a very big problem,” saying it was more important than personal pocketbook issues like inflation and health care affordability. They also ranked it higher than big public policy challenges, such as the federal budget deficit and gun violence, and broader concerns, such as the ability of Democrats and Republicans to work together in Washington. Despite this widespread agreement, grant makers have largely abandoned the issue. When Philanthropy for Active Civic Engagement surveyed its members on which of 13 democracy issues they cared about most, “money in politics/corruption” came in dead last. The more popular choices ranged from “threats to elections” at number one to “centering political identity over everything” at number six.

items.title: Money worries cloud voter mobilization efforts
items.summary: With the midterms approaching, nonprofits work to get out the vote. The Voter Participation Center’s massive voter turnout campaign for the midterm elections almost didn’t happen. “The funding did come, but it was late, very late,” said Tom Lopach, the nonprofit’s president. With big plans but not enough money, Lopach and his staff tried in mid-August to decide what to cut. Should it be a digital get-out-the-vote campaign? A massive effort to get people to vote by mail? Or maybe a “social pressure” push that encourages people to join their peers in casting a ballot? But by the end of summer, money came through, and Lopach and his staff were able to roll out a $40 million effort. The center, which consists of both a 501(c)(3) organization and a 501(c)(4), which can devote money to electoral politics, wants to help 500,000 people submit voter registration applications and 400,000 vote-by-mail applications during the current election cycle. Lopach declined to identify which groups and individuals helped the center stay on track, but in the recent past it has received funding from donor-advised funds at Fidelity Charitable and the Silicon Valley Community Foundation as well as the MacArthur Foundation. Nonprofit leaders have made concerted efforts to encourage democracy-related funding over the past two years, perhaps most notably through the All by April campaign, which helped get philanthropy to dedicate $268 million to a range of issues related to voting, combating misinformation and election administration.

items.title: Why direct mail still delivers at year-end in the age of AI
items.summary: Nonprofits large and small are getting more from the mailbox — and in a world of AI-polished copy, a human touch may be their biggest advantage. For many nonprofits, it’s direct mail go-time. The next few weeks will decide whether the year’s fundraising goals are met, and mail still delivers results — even as organizations devote more resources to online channels. The National Park Foundation’s leaders made a major investment in annual giving three years ago, with ambitious goals for increasing digital revenue. Online fundraising indeed grew, but to the organization’s surprise, direct mail grew even more in dollar terms. Its revenue from direct mail jumped from $17.4 million in 2024 to $28.25 million in the fiscal year that ended September 30, accounting for more than half of the nonprofit’s $48.7 million in annual giving. When asked if AI drove that growth curve, Jennifer Harris, its senior vice president for philanthropy, has an immediate answer: No. But smart tools still have a place in designing a better mail campaign, she says. The Chronicle spoke with fundraisers at nonprofits large and small to learn what’s working in the mailbox this season and where technology enhances value. For two decades, the sector asked whether direct mail would survive the shift to digital. Now the question has evolved, says Dan Sonners, director of direct marketing at the watchdog nonprofit Judicial Watch: “Why is direct mail so persistent? Why does it continue to work against the odds?”

items.title: Veteran charities are highly visible but get less than 1 percent of U.S. giving
items.summary: Top 10 recipients captured 85 percent of 2024’s growth to $4 billion, while older membership groups closed. Nonprofits that serve military members and veterans may be a fixture of television and sports sponsorships, but they receive a relatively small share of U.S. charitable giving. And much of their recent growth went to just a few large organizations, according to a new report. Donations to these groups rose 5.9 percent in 2024, to about $4 billion, before adjusting for inflation, data produced by Indiana University’s Lilly Family School of Philanthropy shows. The findings suggest that the growth may say more about the fundraising strength of a few big organizations than about broad donor enthusiasm. The data also doesn’t capture all of the nuances in a field in which some groups may have seen a narrower or no increase in their fundraising totals, experts said. Military and veteran groups’ share of overall U.S. giving was essentially unchanged. It was 0.68 percent in 2024, the most recent year with finalized IRS figures, and has stayed 0.6 to 0.7 percent for a decade.

items.title: Further Scaling Our Malaria Grantmaking
items.summary: Over the past five years, GiveWell has expanded the scale of our grantmaking and team substantially. We expect to grant more than $1 billion this year, more than double the $418 million we committed in 2025. Alongside this grantmaking growth, we’ve more than doubled the number of researchers on our team since the start of last year. A larger team means we can investigate a greater number of both more complex and larger funding opportunities than we could before. One area where we expect our grantmaking to increase substantially in the coming years is the prevention and treatment of malaria. From 2027 through 2032, we’re aiming to grant at least $2.5 billion in new malaria funding, potentially several times that amount. The total amount will depend on the funding we have available, the feasibility of scaling up cost-effective malaria programs, countries’ appetite for those programs, and how opportunities within malaria compare to other grantmaking areas.
